'''Donald Joseph (D. J.) Newman''' (July 27, 1930 – March 28, 2007) was an American mathematician. He gave simple proofs of the [[prime number theorem]] and the [[Hardy–Ramanujan partition formula]]. He excelled on multiple occasions at the annual [[William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition|Putnam competition]] while studying at [[City College of New York]] and [[New York University]], and later received his PhD from [[Harvard University]] in 1953.<ref>Though [http://genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/html/id.phtml?id=15141 The Math Genealogy Project] lists it as 1958.</ref>

== Life and works ==

Newman was born in [[Brooklyn, New York]], in 1930, and studied at New York's [[Stuyvesant High School]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://65.104.11.121/MathTeam.html |title=Stuyvesant Math Team |accessdate=2007-10-31 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20071001031823/http://65.104.11.121/MathTeam.html |archivedate=2007-10-01 }}</ref> When he was 14 he worked with Dubble Bubble Gum to help solve the statistical question of how often a gum purchaser would receive the same joke for their gum wrapper.<ref>Forrester, Gilda Newman. “Interview about Donald J Newman.” 29 October 2017. Interviewed Newman's sister</ref> He was an avid problem-solver, and as an undergraduate was a [[Putnam Fellow]] all three years he took part in the Putnam math competition; only the third person to attain that feat.<ref>See [http://www.d.umn.edu/~jgallian/putnam05.pdf Joseph Gallian's history of the competition] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061113221122/http://www.d.umn.edu/~jgallian/putnam05.pdf |date=2006-11-13 }} and the official [http://www.maa.org/Awards/putnam.html MAA record]</ref> His mathematical specialties included [[complex analysis]], [[approximation theory]] and [[number theory]]. In 1980 he found a short proof of the [[prime number theorem]], which can now be found in his textbook on ''[[Complex analysis]]''.<ref>Joseph Bak, and D.J.Newman, ''Complex analysis''. ([[Undergraduate Texts in Mathematics]]), Springer Verlag, 3rd edition, 2010.</ref> He also gave a simplified proof of the [[Hardy-Ramanujan partition formula|Hardy-Ramanujans partition formula]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Newman |first=D. J. |date=January 1962 |title=A simplified proof of the partition formula. |journal=Michigan Mathematical Journal |volume=9 |issue=3 |pages=283–287 |doi=10.1307/mmj/1028998729 |issn=0026-2285|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Newman was a friend and associate of [[John Forbes Nash|John Nash]].<ref>{{cite book | last = Nasar | first = Sylvia | title = A Beautiful Mind | url = https://archive.org/details/beautifulmind00sylv | url-access = registration | publisher = Simon & Schuster | location = New York | year = 1998 | isbn = 0-684-85370-1 }}</ref>{{Rp|144–145}} His career included posts as a professor of mathematics at [[MIT]], [[Brown University]], [[Yeshiva University]], [[Temple University]] and a distinguished chair at [[Bar Ilan University]] in Israel.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.temple.edu/newsroom/2006_2007/04/Stories/InMemoriamNewman.html |title=In Memoriam: Donald Newman |accessdate=2008-08-11 |publisher=Temple University |date=2007-04-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080514070949/http://www.temple.edu/newsroom/2006_2007/04/Stories/InMemoriamNewman.html |archive-date=2008-05-14 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Newman's love of problem solving comes through in his writing; his published output as a mathematician includes 150 papers and five books.  He taught numerous students over the years, including [[Robert Feinerman]], [[Jonah Mann]], [[Eli Passow]], [[Louis Raymon]], [[Joseph Bak]], [[Shmuel Weinberger]], and [[Gerald Weinstein]] at Yeshiva University, and Bo Gao, [[Don Kellman]], [[Jonathan Knappenberger]], and Yuan Xu at Temple University.
